Title: A Monday with EducateOS
Voiceover: It’s Monday morning. A teacher has a lesson to prepare, students who need her attention, and no time to learn another complicated system.
Screen_Actions: Open directly into a pre-seeded teacher workspace, not a blank chat. Show course title, the coming lesson and the task the teacher needs to prepare. Start with two seconds of natural cursor motion, no stock footage of children.
On_Screen_Text: `MONDAY, 7:42 A.M.   •   GRADE 7 SCIENCE` and the persistent `SYNTHETIC DISTRICT DEMO` bug.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: A subtle bell-like sound under the first second only; no claim about measured time savings.

Title: A Monday with EducateOS
Voiceover: She starts with an approved resource, chooses what students should learn, and builds a water-quality investigation. Students won't see material that hasn't gone through the school's review process.
Screen_Actions: Select sample learning objective → open approved resource with provenance/approval state → create or preview an investigation. Cut out idle time but show the meaningful approval checkpoint; do not morph a draft magically into a published class activity.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: If current UI requires seeded content rather than an end-to-end creation flow, label this scene `ILLUSTRATIVE FLOW FROM SYNTHETIC FIXTURES`.

Title: A Monday with EducateOS
Voiceover: A student opens the activity, studies the evidence, and works through an answer. Where AI help is enabled, it follows boundaries chosen by the school—not whatever a chatbot decides on its own.
Screen_Actions: Switch to the synthetic student profile and show assignment directions, data table and draft explanation. If an AI conversation is not live on the pinned build, use only the assignment/workspace view and let the sentence about AI play over a clearly labeled policy diagram.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Use synthetic artifacts only. A policy test alone is not proof that every student chat route is protected end to end.

Title: A Monday with EducateOS
Voiceover: When the assignment comes back, EducateOS can help organize feedback and propose a score. But a suggestion isn't a grade. The teacher reviews, changes, rejects, or approves what becomes official.
Screen_Actions: Teacher submission view → suggested feedback → teacher edits → separate approval control → approved state. Prefer a fresh, repeatable capture; otherwise record the genuine tested service behavior with a `SYNTHETIC TEST` tag.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Do not show AI autopublishing. Hold two seconds on the human approval.

Title: A Monday with EducateOS
Voiceover: District leaders set the permissions, manage AI spending, and decide which connections are allowed. The classroom gets useful tools; the school keeps the guardrails.
Screen_Actions: Admin policy or budget view → integration health or configured capability → back to teacher view. Use only actual UI fields demonstrated on this build; an annotated synthetic evidence screenshot is acceptable if labeled.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Never claim FERPA certification or completed accessibility validation from this shot.

Title: A Monday with EducateOS
Voiceover: And EducateOS is open source. A school organization can run it in its own cloud account, with its own data and its own operating decisions.
Screen_Actions: Clean diagram: boundary around `SCHOOL CLOUD ACCOUNT` containing runtime/data; separate `OPTIONAL FOUNDATION SUPPORT` outside the boundary. Do not show Clever as a signed foundation partner.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Cloudflare/provider fees still exist; “open source” means no mandatory EducateOS software license.

Title: A Monday with EducateOS
Voiceover: We're inviting educators and technology leaders to shape the first pilots. See what we've built. Tell us what your school really needs.
Screen_Actions: Return to actual lesson thumbnail, then product lockup, short readable URL and QR to one preview-request page. Hold end card at least two seconds.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Do not suggest pilots are already operating with real student data.

Title: From standard to classroom activity
Voiceover: Imagine you teach seventh-grade science. Tomorrow, students will investigate why a stream’s water quality changed after a storm. You have learning standards to meet, a reading your school has approved, and students who need different kinds of help. Usually those ingredients live in different places. Let's see what it takes to turn them into one useful activity here.
Screen_Actions: Open teacher workspace in the synthetic class. The lesson banner reads `Water Quality: Claims and Evidence`; show objective summary. Never start from an empty generalized agent chat.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Use a genuinely populated sample class. Any standards ID on screen must be verified against the catalog; otherwise show a descriptive learning objective without a code.

Title: From standard to classroom activity
Voiceover: First I pick the instructional target. Notice the order: we are not asking an AI system to invent our curriculum. The objective comes from the school's selected framework. Here, I want students to compare measurements, make a claim, and explain what evidence supports it. I can then select the resources approved for that goal, with their provenance and version visible.
Screen_Actions: Open curriculum catalog → inspect a standards/competency record → choose an approved resource → pause over source/provenance/version. Use two close-up inserts so the text is readable.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Don't say a specific state agency certified this content or granted blanket reuse rights unless documented.

Title: From standard to classroom activity
Voiceover: Now say I bring in a worksheet or an article that isn't in the catalog yet. That material should not become trusted classroom content just because I pasted a link. EducateOS has a review step. I inspect the source, check that we're allowed to use it, and decide whether it belongs in this activity. Only the approved release becomes material students can encounter. That checkpoint is part of teaching responsibly with AI.
Screen_Actions: Import a benign sample document → show quarantined/review status → open review → approve an immutable resource version. If capturing separate takes, label crossfade `Time compressed`.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: A reviewer can still make a bad decision; don't promise the review catches every malicious document or rights problem.

Title: From standard to classroom activity
Voiceover: Next I use the investigation template. Students will look at upstream and downstream measurements, identify the strongest evidence, and explain what else they would want to know before reaching a conclusion. I can preview the student instructions and revise the success criteria. If AI suggests language for a rubric, I still choose what counts as strong reasoning. The assignment is mine to teach.
Screen_Actions: Choose science-investigation template → edit title/questions → show a small synthetic measurement table → preview student experience → adjust criteria. If rubric editor isn't live, put `ILLUSTRATIVE RUBRIC PREVIEW` on the insert.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: No blanket claim of accommodations, screen-reader compliance or fully automated standard alignment.

Title: From standard to classroom activity
Voiceover: Let's switch to a fictional student. They see the task in their own course workspace, not an administrator's screen. They read the measurements, write a claim, and attach the evidence they chose. If the school has enabled AI help for the class, a useful response is one that helps the student think: What pattern do you notice? What measurement might change your conclusion? It should not simply write their answer for them.
Screen_Actions: Sign in as student → open assigned activity → enter a short original response → save a draft and submit. If a tested assistant is available, show one thoughtful question and response; otherwise use static policy explainer over real work view.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: AI pedagogical quality is a design goal, not a guaranteed outcome.

Title: From standard to classroom activity
Voiceover: Back in the teacher account, I can inspect what the student submitted. A feedback draft might call out one strong argument and one gap in the evidence. I can edit that comment, reject a suggestion I disagree with, or decide no score is appropriate yet. If an official grade is going to be recorded, it goes through a distinct teacher decision. This protects teacher judgment without discarding useful assistance.
Screen_Actions: Open submission → inspect possible feedback proposal → manually change a sentence → approve or reject in a separate action. Record a real persisted status. Capture a second version where the teacher chooses `Not ready` or a genuine equivalent.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: The domain grading gate and the precise current teacher UI must both be checked; don't fabricate button labels.

Title: From standard to classroom activity
Voiceover: If the school already uses Canvas, this does not need to be an LMS replacement project. The approved result can use the district's configured LTI connection and appear in the Canvas gradebook. We've exercised that handoff in a real Canvas test environment. Other platforms need their own connector validation; we don't pretend one test automatically covers every LMS.
Screen_Actions: Show genuine Canvas lab launch → approved test grade in EducateOS → resulting Canvas test gradebook. If current lab isn't accessible, use a diagram labeled `Canvas lab-tested Oct 2026`, never a recreated vendor screen shown as live.
On_Screen_Text: `CANVAS: TESTED LTI GRADE PASSBACK` / `NO CERTIFICATION CLAIM`.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: LMS tool-side LTI Advantage features are externally lab-tested; 1EdTech certification has not been obtained.

Title: From standard to classroom activity
Voiceover: A Michigan district, a Texas district, and a small independent school may have very different standards, course structures, and learning platforms. They don't need identical curricula to benefit from the same flow: an approved objective, a trusted resource, an activity students can understand, and a teacher accountable for the result. The technology should adapt to a school's practice—not the other way around.
Screen_Actions: Three synthetic configuration cards for different school types, then return to the shared workflow. Show only configuration features already implemented or clearly annotate as illustrative.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: No real Michigan or Texas district is being portrayed as a customer.

Title: From standard to classroom activity
Voiceover: Where would you want one less click? Where should a teacher have more control? And what would make this genuinely useful on a busy Tuesday? We're assembling a founding educator advisory group to answer exactly those questions. We'd love to show you the working demo and hear your objections.
Screen_Actions: End on student preview and teacher edit state. Fade to a single link for educator advisory requests.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Invite advice, not endorsement or purchase commitment.

Title: Your district. Your cloud account.
Voiceover: Before we look at an AI feature, let's answer the first technical question: whose system is this? EducateOS is open-source software designed to run in the school organization's own Cloudflare account. The foundation's proposed role is to coordinate shared standards, integrations, and support—not to own the district's student records or decide its instructional policy.
Screen_Actions: Simple trust-boundary diagram. One enclosed district account contains runtime/storage/admins. External IdP/SIS/LMS and proposed foundation broker sit outside. Highlight arrows by data category, not cartoon server icons.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Show this as the architectural model, not as proof the first district deployment has passed full production acceptance.

Title: Your district. Your cloud account.
Voiceover: In a test installation, we can inspect the resources running in that account, the administrators allowed to operate them, and the integrations configured for its identity and courses. The optional foundation control plane should not sit in the middle of an ordinary student's assignment. But every centrally operated connector still needs a defined failure mode, a security owner, and an exit plan. Those details belong in the district agreement.
Screen_Actions: Open demo Cloudflare project with account and token details redacted → highlight the district worker and storage namespace → show simplified request path. If the account is the developer-owned demo tenant, clearly call it `PROJECT-OWNED TEST ACCOUNT`, not a school-owned production account.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: No assertion that a foundation Clever broker is operational or contracted.

Title: Your district. Your cloud account.
Voiceover: School identity gets complicated fast. People change schools. Teachers teach across buildings. Two providers may report different identifiers, and an email address can be reused. EducateOS links a verified provider identity to a principal inside a particular district. The effective key is district, issuer, and subject. Then local authorization determines what that person can access. We want a repeated name in two districts to stay two separate identities.
Screen_Actions: Diagram `(district, issuer, subject) → principal`. Show the synthetic same-name / cross-district fixture and its denied request result; distinguish policy tests from live production boundaries.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Do not claim unimplemented private-chat API routes passed end-to-end isolation tests.

Title: Your district. Your cloud account.
Voiceover: Now rosters. A bad synchronization should not erase a school's history or treat a broken upstream feed as a mass withdrawal. In the synthetic roster test, an unexpectedly large removal is held for administrator review. It gives staff time to investigate the feed before applying the change. That's the behavior we want whether the source is a CSV, OneRoster service, or an authorized commercial integration.
Screen_Actions: Open synthetic roster import/diff; execute a real test producing `removal-held` → show the exact confirmation step if available. If the console lacks a hold UI, show the test output with `HARNESS TEST` banner instead of constructing a fake console.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: As of repo maturity dated Oct 26, Clever full roster permissions were not available live and ClassLink remained provider-fake-tested. Do not show those flows as production.

Title: Your district. Your cloud account.
Voiceover: Governance also has to be operational. The district needs to decide who may use an AI capability, what it can cost, and which actions require a person's approval. In our test paths, spending limits and approval policies are enforced by code rather than left as a paragraph in an acceptable-use policy. But a domain-level test doesn't automatically mean the full administrator interface has passed every acceptance test.
Screen_Actions: Budget configuration; permitted and refused synthetic calls; a teacher-approved grade path. Overlay small labels `CODE TEST` or `LIVE UI` on each clip. Pause on the actual refusal and on the actual approval.
On_Screen_Text: `WHO CAN ACT?  HOW MUCH CAN IT SPEND?  WHO APPROVES?`.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: G1 synthetic pilot gate still contains open end-to-end criteria; call them out in companion handout.

Title: Your district. Your cloud account.
Voiceover: We have exercised EducateOS as an LTI 1.3 tool against actual Canvas and Moodle environments. Those lab runs included authenticated launches, course membership reads, Deep Linking responses, and teacher-approved grades passed to the external gradebook. That is meaningful interoperability evidence. It is not formal 1EdTech certification, and it does not mean every vendor combination has completed integration testing.
Screen_Actions: Use real test captures with date/version bug. Show Canvas or Moodle test course launching the tool and the resulting grade change. For Deep Linking, distinguish verified response from an end-user picker interaction if the latter was not captured live.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Never use a certification emblem or vendor logo as an implied endorsement.

Title: Your district. Your cloud account.
Voiceover: Then comes day two. Who notices a failed sync? Who rotates credentials? Can we revoke someone's access after a roster change? Who restores a lost environment? Who gets called if a foundation-operated service is down? We have a pilot gate that records the tests we can run and the tests still missing. Accessibility, some production integrations, and a real recovery rehearsal must be settled before a school depends on the full system.
Screen_Actions: Show test/status matrix `MET / OPEN` with source links. Rotate through integration health, logged test result, restore checklist. Do not create a fake 24/7 status page.
On_Screen_Text: `OPERATIONAL READINESS IS A TEST, NOT A SLOGAN`.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Show a few real unresolved items, not a misleading green wall of checkmarks.

Title: Your district. Your cloud account.
Voiceover: A school should not have to surrender its data or take on a mandatory EducateOS license to use the software. The foundation model is designed around shared maintenance and optional services, while the school pays its own infrastructure costs. We also need to spell out what happens if a district stops using a foundation-operated connection: which data can be exported, which credentials are revoked, and what continues working locally.
Screen_Actions: Show license file and district-owned infrastructure box. A contract-boundary diagram identifies proposed foundation services and optional support order. If export is not end-to-end validated on current build, display an `EXIT PLAN UNDER VALIDATION` callout.
On_Screen_Text: `FREE SOFTWARE LICENSE • DISTRICT CLOUD COSTS • OPTIONAL SERVICES`.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Don't imply Clever has approved the proposed umbrella contract, delegated credentials or foundation pricing.

Title: Your district. Your cloud account.
Voiceover: We welcome the hard questions. Try a stale roster. Rotate a key. Bring an identity collision. Ask us to demonstrate a denied access request, a vendor outage, and an actual restore. What we can't prove yet should become a test plan—not a marketing claim. That's how we want the first districts to help us build a system they can trust.
Screen_Actions: Fast grid of concrete test cases with `PROVEN IN LAB`, `SYNTHETIC TEST`, or `OPEN` labels, one per case. Display link to current maturity matrix.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Use a consistent source date and commit reference in a lower-third or end appendix.

Title: Your district. Your cloud account.
Voiceover: If you lead school technology, we'd like forty-five minutes to show you the code, the running system, and the unfinished gates. Help us decide what truly needs to be ready for the first district pilot.
Screen_Actions: Product lockup and a single technical-review link; visual preview of architecture/evidence packet; no student information requested on the form.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Advisory involvement is not a vendor endorsement.

Title: Fits your existing LMS
Voiceover: You already have a learning management system. Teachers know where their courses live, students know where assignments appear, and your district has invested years making it work. EducateOS should fit that environment—not demand that you replace it.
Screen_Actions: Begin in a real Canvas sandbox course. Show EducateOS as an installed external tool within the course. Do not open with an EducateOS admin screen.
On_Screen_Text: `KEEP YOUR LMS. ADD CONTROLLED AI WORKFLOWS.`
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Label `CANVAS TEST ENVIRONMENT`; it is not an actual district customer's account.

Title: Fits your existing LMS
Voiceover: Let's start with a teacher launching the tool from Canvas. The launch tells EducateOS which platform and course this request came from. EducateOS validates the signed context and maps it to the district's existing course and person. It doesn't assume a name or email address is enough to grant access.
Screen_Actions: Click a tested Canvas course-navigation placement → show launch → briefly zoom on educator's assigned course. Insert small animation `LTI SIGNED LAUNCH → DISTRICT PRINCIPAL`, not a simulated credential window.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: LTI tool-side launch passed live Canvas/Moodle tests. Capture current repeatable run.

Title: Fits your existing LMS
Voiceover: Now suppose the teacher has built our water-quality investigation. Instead of sending students to hunt for a separate link, the district can use LTI Deep Linking to associate that activity with its LMS course. The teacher chooses the content, the platform returns a link, and students can encounter the activity in the place they already work.
Screen_Actions: Show activity picker/configuration in EducateOS → capture the verified Deep Linking response, then show the resulting test assignment placed through the documented Canvas lab method. Label `RETURN RESPONSE VERIFIED; PLACEMENT CAPTURED VIA LAB API` if the interactive picker could not be clicked end-to-end.

Title: Fits your existing LMS
Voiceover: The student opens the linked activity in its course context and submits work. The teacher can review it within EducateOS, use whatever feedback assistance is enabled, and approve the consequential result. That review step is important: the AI's proposal is not automatically the score that travels into the school record.

Title: Fits your existing LMS
Voiceover: Here's the part an LMS administrator wants to see. After the teacher approves a grade and the district has configured Canvas as the authority for that course, EducateOS uses the LTI Assignment and Grade Services connection. In our live lab, the result made it into the Canvas gradebook. We also tested the underlying LTI Advantage service path with Moodle. That's a real integration milestone, with a defined test scope.
Screen_Actions: Split-screen test approval and resulting gradebook entry with controlled time match. Brief overlay of `AGS` and `NRPS` as service labels, not broad product badges. Show a lab request ID or source evidence link at bottom for technical audiences.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: No formal 1EdTech certification; don't extrapolate to all Canvas tenants or Schoology.

Title: Fits your existing LMS
Voiceover: Not every school uses Canvas. The architecture also includes a Schoology-oriented LTI configuration and separate Google Classroom API work. Google Classroom isn't simply another standard LTI launch. We've exercised a small live Classroom coursework-and-grade flow, but not a district-wide production roster. Clever and ClassLink have separate identity and rostering paths, which still need fuller live validation.

Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: The Schoology-flavored test platform is synthetic; no verified live Schoology claim without new evidence.

Title: Fits your existing LMS
Voiceover: The key district decision is authority. Which system owns enrollment? Which one is allowed to issue an official grade? Does a student sign in through Google, Clever, ClassLink, or a district identity provider? EducateOS treats those as separate configuration questions. That's deliberate, because one school can have several of these products at the same time.
Screen_Actions: Show editable or diagrammed matrix `Identity / Roster / Course / Grade of record` for one fictional school, with actual configured example values. Animate arrows individually; avoid showing passwords and OAuth client secrets.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: This is an architectural separation, not evidence every provider combination is supported in production.

Title: Fits your existing LMS
Voiceover: If you're responsible for Canvas, Schoology, Google Classroom, or the district roster, we'd like to review your current workflow with you. Bring the configuration you actually use. We'll show the tested path, identify the gaps, and decide whether EducateOS fits without disrupting your teachers.
Screen_Actions: Show the integration matrix with one row per platform, then end on `Request an interoperability review` and a simple vendor-neutral workflow diagram.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Technical discussion only, not a request for production student credentials or data.

Title: What AI is allowed to do
Voiceover: A school shouldn't have to choose between useful AI and control over student work. The important question isn't only what an AI model can generate. It's what the system lets it see, what it's allowed to change, and who can intervene when something goes wrong.
Screen_Actions: Start on a student's sample assignment; zoom out to a simple permission boundary between student, teacher, administrator and assistant. Avoid ominous stock images of students under surveillance.
On_Screen_Text: `WHO CAN SEE?  WHO CAN ACT?  WHO CAN OVERRIDE?`.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Do not claim the software makes all model outputs safe or correct.

Title: What AI is allowed to do
Voiceover: Take two students in the same class. They may see the same instructions, but that doesn't give one student permission to open the other's private draft. A teacher should see assigned work that needs review—not a blanket window into everything a student thinks or types. Access follows the verified person and the task they're authorized to perform.
Screen_Actions: Show synthetic requests for class activity and another student's artifact. Capture a tested API refusal for the artifact. If private AI chat protection is shown, label it `POLICY-LEVEL TEST ONLY` unless the specific live route has since passed.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: The October pilot gate still marks private-chat API route coverage incomplete; don't show it as production-proven.

Title: What AI is allowed to do
Scene: 00:45–01:15 — An agent can't make a secret grade decision
Voiceover: Now imagine an AI assistant suggests a score or feedback. That recommendation may help a teacher, but it does not grant the assistant authority to publish an official grade. In the tested assessment path, consequential grade writes are separated from the proposal and routed through teacher approval. The point is accountability: a person owns the educational decision.
Screen_Actions: Synthetic grading flow with a proposed score → teacher changes it → official-grade approval. If only domain test path exists, label `ASSESSMENT SERVICE TEST` and avoid manufacturing a teacher console interaction.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Some end-to-end pilot grade-gate routes remain open; be precise about tested layer.

Title: What AI is allowed to do
Voiceover: Permissions also include money and capabilities. A school may decide which classes receive a particular AI tool, what its budget is, and how it should behave when that budget is exhausted. EducateOS is being built so these choices are enforceable and visible to the people responsible for them—not buried in a vendor setting nobody checks.
Screen_Actions: Show synthetic course budget and test a budget-denied AI request. Then show policy revision/approval only if the user-facing path is working; otherwise display `tested policy service` overlay.
On_Screen_Text: `SCOPE IT • LIMIT IT • AUDIT THE DECISION`.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Cost figures shown are demo seeds, not district estimates or guaranteed billing limits across all providers.

Title: What AI is allowed to do
Voiceover: Governance also means admitting that systems fail. A provider might be unavailable, a roster might be wrong, or an imported document might contain instructions it should never have carried. The right behavior is to surface the problem, preserve an audit trail where appropriate, and stop unsafe changes until a person can review them. That is the standard we want schools to test with us.
Screen_Actions: Sequence: provider health error from synthetic harness → held large roster removal → imported-resource review flag. Do not add a fictitious safety incident or show real student discussions as training fodder.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Hall Monitor deployment and exact incident workflows need separate product evidence; do not imply comprehensive student surveillance.

Title: What AI is allowed to do
Voiceover: No responsible vendor should ask a district to accept a promise of perfect AI safety. We can show the boundaries we've tested, the gaps still on the pilot checklist, and the choices each school controls. We're inviting school leaders to challenge those assumptions in a supervised demo, before any real student records enter the picture.
Screen_Actions: Short evidence ledger: `Verified lab / Synthetic test / Open gate`. Finish with one CTA and a very small privacy/safety FAQ link on the landing page, not a second on-video CTA.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: No 'FERPA certified', 'COPPA certified', 'zero risk', or blanket zero-retention claim.

Title: Small school, small IT burden
Voiceover: If you're running technology for a small school, you probably don't have a department for every system. You may be the person managing Chromebooks, accounts, the gradebook, classroom apps—and the Wi-Fi. A new tool that arrives with six integration projects isn't helping.
Screen_Actions: Start with a fictional school administrator dashboard and an unobtrusive line `One technology coordinator. Many jobs.` No stock images of overworked children or teachers.
On_Screen_Text: `BUILT WITH SMALL SCHOOL TEAMS IN MIND`.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: No claim of fully automated no-code install unless the path passes a fresh-account test.

Title: Small school, small IT burden
Voiceover: In our synthetic small-school example, there is no expensive SIS contract to integrate. The school can start with a local directory or a roster it controls, define a few classes, and decide where official grades will live. It doesn't need to buy Clever just to try the EducateOS classroom model. If the school already runs Google Workspace, that's another configuration we can evaluate.
Screen_Actions: Show Prairie synthetic school selection; local/manual roster with synthetic names; one class and configured grade authority. Optional cut to Harbor Google profile explicitly labeled as a separate test scenario.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Manual roster sync and local auth behavior must be freshly checked in running UI; never imply every small school can avoid paid infra.

Title: Small school, small IT burden
Voiceover: A school administrator would choose its cloud account, confirm its domain, select a sign-in method, and review the initial permissions. Then it connects—or imports—the class directory and establishes an AI budget. We want that to be a guided process with understandable warnings. Where a step still needs engineering or vendor approval, it should say so rather than send someone into a maze.
Screen_Actions: Guided installer or setup preview. For unvalidated steps, use explanatory cards labeled `INSTALLER PREVIEW`, not a seamless fake install. Show permission preview, domain, roster, budget in sequence; avoid untested `one-click` language.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Current code includes guided-install work but production self-service acceptance is not finished.

Title: Small school, small IT burden
Voiceover: After setup, the teacher shouldn't become a cloud operator. They open their class, choose an approved resource, and teach. The school maintains the account and its policies. If it needs someone to handle initial configuration, training, or a difficult integration, those services can be purchased separately rather than being bundled into a mandatory software subscription.
Screen_Actions: Teacher lesson creation → student view → compact cost/ownership card. Only show actual optional-services offering as a proposal; don't show a fictitious checkout receipt.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: District/provider usage charges and operational responsibility remain. Exact optional support pricing is proposed, not published contract pricing.

Title: Small school, small IT burden
Voiceover: The result we're aiming for is simple: a small school can make its own decisions without hiring a cloud engineering team for every change. We still need small-school administrators to pressure-test the setup and the support plan. If that's your world, we'd love to walk through it together and find out where it feels too complicated.
Screen_Actions: Show one-page `small-school deployment checklist` and one preview-request URL. End on the actual synthetic school home.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Never promise a self-hosted system needs zero maintenance.

Title: The foundation model in plain English
Voiceover: Most school software works the same way: you subscribe, use someone else's system, and hope the product keeps serving your school. EducateOS begins with a different assumption: the school should be able to own and operate its own instance.
Screen_Actions: Side-by-side: `Conventional hosted app` (school arrows into vendor tenant) versus `District-owned EducateOS` (school boundary around runtime and data). No specific competitor logo.
On_Screen_Text: `THE SOFTWARE RUNS IN YOUR SCHOOL'S ACCOUNT`.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: No assertion that a vendor literally owns student records under every SaaS agreement; focus on hosting/control model.

Title: The foundation model in plain English
Voiceover: The EducateOS code is open source. A district or independent school can deploy it in an account it controls, make local policy choices, and keep the student data under its own administration. The school still pays its cloud, AI, and any outside provider costs. Open source does not mean running technology is free.
Screen_Actions: Show `Open-source license: $0` card, then a distinct `District cloud and AI usage: district pays provider` card. Use unpriced arrows rather than invented monthly estimates.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: District-owned Cloudflare costs may be variable; do not imply all third-party integrations are free.

Title: The foundation model in plain English
Voiceover: The proposed EducateOS Foundation would help maintain shared software, interoperability standards, releases, documentation, and relationships with providers. Instead of every district reinventing the same integrations, participating schools could benefit from shared coordination while retaining control of their own deployment.
Screen_Actions: Draw foundation as a ring around shared engineering, knowledge base, integration review, and policy templates; district installations remain separate. Lines are support or authorization, not centralized student-data pipelines.
Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: Foundation legal status and agreements are proposed, not finalized.

Title: The foundation model in plain English
Voiceover: A school could choose optional setup, training, or support services under a separate agreement. Shared integration costs need sustainable funding. Title: Complete product tour with anticipated Q&A

The intuitive approach would be paste the link, press Generate, and hope. But a web page can change. A PDF can contain misleading instructions. Rights can differ. So this material enters a review flow. The teacher—or whoever the school has designated—looks at it, verifies that it belongs in the class and that the reuse conditions make sense, and publishes an approved version. The version can then be referenced by activities without silently changing when the source website does. Notice the separation here: the assistant may help organize content, but content isn't allowed to turn itself into trusted school policy. The reviewer decides.

Title: Complete product tour with anticipated Q&A

Title: Complete product tour with anticipated Q&A

I can reject a suggestion that doesn't fit the lesson. If a score is appropriate, the assessment path distinguishes a proposal from an official grade. The decision to publish belongs to the authorized teacher. Choose a domain that the district also controls; that makes identity, certificates and exit planning easier to reason about. Before clicking Install, confirm who can approve DNS changes, who is authorized to deploy Workers, and where the billing alerts go. We want a named primary administrator and a backup—not a single staff member's personal login as the school's disaster-recovery plan. In this test, I'll use our synthetic organization's account and domain, which are not a real school's resources.

Title: Installation and support clinic
Voiceover: Next are installation permissions. This is where many systems ask for far more access than they need. The installer should present what resources it intends to create or change. We need to understand whether a token can deploy Workers, modify routes, access storage, or update DNS. Here I review the plan before authorizing it. I also check that the credentials are scoped, that there's a route to revoke them, and that the production runtime won't rely on an installation credential staying active forever. If I revoke installer authorization midway through an upgrade, the safe outcome is to stop making new changes and preserve the running school system—not to continue with a partially trusted session.

Editorial_and_Evidence_Gate: The revoked-installer-credential safety path is exercised in tests; live cloud permissions still require their own runbook validation.

Title: Installation and support clinic
Scene: 02:30–03:30 — Apply, validate, and record what changed

First check that the health endpoint responds, that the expected runtime and storage exist, and that an unauthenticated visitor cannot simply open a private district API. We also need to verify the public endpoints an LMS legitimately requires, such as its LTI key discovery path. This is the stage where a good installer either produces evidence or produces a concrete error we can fix.

Show a private API denied to an anonymous browser and a public JWKS endpoint permitted if the current deployment supports it. A classroom teacher shouldn't accidentally inherit these permissions because they happen to use the same email address at another school. The first sign-in is a test: a valid administrator reaches the console, and someone with the wrong identity or role does not.

If the school wants Clever, we need to confirm whether the intended connection is an ordinary portal link, a full OAuth integration, or a production roster authorization; the proposed foundation umbrella contract is not yet a substitute for vendor approval.

We check the provider status, the connector's configured scopes, and the last known successful sync. We record the error without exposing credentials, keep the current safe roster state, and escalate if the school cannot correct the authorization. That is the kind of routine failure a school should be able to understand from documentation before opening a support ticket.

A problem in a foundation-operated broker has a separate incident owner, because that service is the foundation's responsibility.
